topic: Dandelin Spheres: The Geometric Secret of Conic Sections
target_audience: High school students and early university undergraduates

sections.title: The Mystery of the Slanted Slice
sections.content: Introduction to the concept of conic sections. We define an ellipse not just as a 'squashed circle,' but as the intersection of a plane and a double cone. The central question: How do we prove that this 3D intersection matches the 2D algebraic definition of an ellipse (the sum of distances to two foci is constant)?
sections.example: Visualize a laser-cutting robot slicing through a giant orange traffic cone at an angle. The resulting edge is a perfect ellipse, but where are its hidden 'foci'?

sections.title: Prerequisite: The 'Ice Cream' Property
sections.content: Before the proof, we must understand a fundamental property of spheres: Tangent segments from a single point to a sphere are always equal in length. This is a crucial 'Lego brick' for our geometric construction.
sections.example: Imagine a spherical scoop of ice cream sitting in a cone. If you measure the distance from the bottom tip of the cone to any point where the ice cream touches the cone's side, that distance is always the same, forming a perfect circle of contact.

sections.title: The Dandelin Construction
sections.content: Introducing Germinal Dandelin's 1822 breakthrough. We place two spheres of different sizes inside the cone: one above the cutting plane and one below. Each sphere must be tangent to the cone (touching it in a circle) and tangent to the plane at exactly one point ($F_1$ and $F_2$).
sections.example: Think of two transparent bubbles expanding inside a glass cone until they get 'stuck' against the slanted cutting plane. The points where they 'kiss' the plane are our focal points.

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: The Proof
sections.content: Pick any point $P$ on the ellipse. Draw lines from $P$ to the two contact points $F_1$ and $F_2$. By using the 'Ice Cream Property' from Section 2, we show that $PF_1$ and $PF_2$ are equal to segments along the cone's surface. The sum $PF_1 + PF_2$ equals the constant distance between the two circles of contact.
sections.example: An animated spider crawls along the edge of the ellipse. As it moves, two colored strings (representing $PF_1$ and $PF_2$) change length, but their total length remains constant, perfectly tracing the geometric definition of an ellipse.

sections.title: Universal Geometry: Parabolas and Hyperbolas
sections.content: Conclude by showing how this isn't just for ellipses. By tilting the cutting plane to be parallel to the cone's side, or cutting through both halves of a double cone, the Dandelin Spheres still identify the foci for parabolas and hyperbolas.
sections.example: A lighthouse beam (cone) hitting the ocean surface (plane). If the beam is parallel to the water, the light patch is a parabola; if it tilts further, it becomes a hyperbola. The Dandelin spheres 'float' inside the beam to mark the path of the light.
